clue.text: Snack service, one in wrapper ready for delivery

indicators.note: in tells us the service and the one sit inside the wrapper

parts.note: an SAE is a stamped addressed envelope, a wrapper already set up for posting
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone describes a catering service that hands each customer a packaged item ready to be sent out.
explanation.walkthrough: SARNIE is British slang for a sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich is a quick light meal eaten between main ones, so it counts as a snack.

clue.text: Long slice of feta cheese

indicators.note: a slice is a piece cut out of something, so a run of letters is taken from inside these two words

explanation.surface: A recipe asks for a generous, lengthy piece cut from a block of Greek cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for the slice; it is a verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something and to ache for it both mean to want it badly.

clue.text: Learned books sustain latest paper supplier

indicators.note: in a down clue the later pieces stand under the first and hold it up, so they sustain it

parts.note: the latest thing is the new one
a learned person is a sage, and sage can be an adjective meaning wise
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Scholarly volumes are said to keep the most recent newspaper going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' looks like a past tense verb but is the adjective (two syllables) meaning wise.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop that sells newspapers and magazines is the usual retailer of papers.

clue.text: Nauseating article turns up in English clubs

indicators.note: in shows the reversed article sits between the English and the clubs letters

parts.note: C is the card-game abbreviation for the suit of clubs

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: an item is an article, as in an article in a list or newspaper

explanation.surface: A sickening story appears in the papers about English golf or card clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' suggests a grammatical article such as THE or AN; here it is ITEM.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic substance makes a person vomit, so it is literally sickening.

clue.text: Bangers, nuts and bananas not all there

definitions.meaning: Christmas ... are pulled to go off with a bang
to go bananas is to go mad, so bananas means crazy
someone not all there is mentally unbalanced, mad

explanation.surface: A shopping list of sausages, nuts and bananas is missing some items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bangers' looks like British slang for sausages; here it is party crackers that go bang when pulled. Three of the four definitions all mean mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is both a festive novelty that pops and a slang word meaning insane, as with nuts, bananas and not all there.

clue.text: Novice once fed on random microwave meals?

indicators.note: something random has no set order, so these letters are rearranged at will

explanation.surface: A beginner who once ate whatever came along now lives on ready meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready meals that need only heating in a microwave are the classic kind of quick processed eating.

clue.text: Charlie avoids habit-forming preservative for one

indicators.note: avoids says the Charlie letter keeps out, so it is dropped from the word

parts.note: a habit-forming drug is an addictive one
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie keeps away from a preservative because it is addictive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is also slang for cocaine, which fits the drug surface but here is just C.
explanation.definitionFit: Preservatives are substances added to food, an example of the broader class of such ingredients, as signalled by 'for one'.

clue.text: Ford place out of commission

parts.note: the Ka is a small car made by Ford
to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: A Ford car's spot is out of service, or a Ford is parked broken down.
explanation.definitionFit: Something kaput is broken and no longer working, the same as being out of service.

clue.text: About to tour St Petersburg once, start off in reverse

indicators.note: to tour is to go round, so the about letters go around the rest

parts.note: RE means about or concerning, as in letters

indicators.note: start off means the first letter of the city name is removed

parts.note: St Petersburg was called Petrograd from 1914 to 1924

explanation.surface: Someone is about to visit the old Russian capital, but sets off backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'About to' as a single phrase meaning ready to; the parse splits it, RE being 'About' and 'to tour' being the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrograde motion is backward movement, going in the opposite direction.

clue.text: Dog gets my German dish

parts.note: a chow is a breed of dog from China
mein is the German word for my

explanation.surface: A dog snaffles a German person's meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fried noodles with meat or vegetables are a well-known Chinese restaurant meal.

clue.text: Number Two's tax disc sent in

indicators.note: sent in means one piece is put inside another

parts.note: a duty is a tax on goods
an EP is an extended play record, a disc

explanation.surface: A second-in-command hands in a tax disc, the old British car tax certificate.
explanation.walkthrough: A tax disc was the paper circle once shown on British car windscreens; here 'tax' and 'disc' are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A second-in-command, the one who stands in for the boss, is commonly called a number two.

clue.text: A fruit tree's top in country food

parts.note: a lime is a citrus fruit

indicators.note: in says the tree's first letter goes inside the country

parts.note: a nation is a country

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fruit tree's crown appears in a country's food supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Alimentation is nourishment, the supply of nutrients, which is what food provides.

clue.text: Relish top northern booze

parts.note: the brow is the top of a hill
the sauce is slang for alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Someone praises the finest northern drink.
explanation.walkthrough: BROWN SAUCE is a dark, tangy British table sauce, such as HP.
explanation.definitionFit: A relish is a tangy condiment, and this dark spicy table sauce is one.

clue.text: It's put on 24 and 16

parts.note: the clue points to two other answers in the grid, savoury biscuits, onto which a soft cheese is spread

explanation.surface: A cross-reference saying something is placed on top of two other answers.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers refer to other entries in the printed grid, such as the oatcakes clue; a soft French cheese is what goes on top of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft French cheese is commonly spread on biscuits such as oatcakes and crackers.

clue.text: They conquer lady's heart in stylish short poem

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing

indicators.note: in shows the heart of the lady goes inside the shortened poem
short means the poem's last letter is cut

parts.note: a verse is a poem

indicators.note: the heart of the word lady is its central pair of letters

explanation.surface: Some romantic conquerors win a woman over with a smart little poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conquer' looks like a verb in a love story, but 'They conquer' is the definition; 'short' removes the poem's final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Invaders are those who march into and take over territory, people who conquer.

clue.text: Countless flyers imported, all about milk supplier

indicators.note: all about means the whole combination is turned round and read backwards
imported says the flyers are brought inside the countless word

parts.note: myriad means countless, too many to count
the RAF is the Royal Air Force, whose members fly

explanation.surface: Countless birds have been brought in, all to do with milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flyers' suggests birds; it is the Royal Air Force. 'all about' reverses the entire assembled string, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm that keeps cows for milking is where milk comes from, so it supplies milk.

clue.text: Copper's suggested faster route

parts.note: read as wordplay, ... means the word cut shortened, CU, which is the chemical symbol for copper, so copper is what the phrase suggests

explanation.surface: A police officer has proposed a quicker way to get somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, taken as wordplay, makes the clue words. Shorten CUT and you get CU, copper's symbol. 'Copper' looks like a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A short cut is a quicker way than the usual road, a faster route.

clue.text: Start with yen lad's saved

indicators.note: saved means kept safe inside, so the son holds the other letters

parts.note: a son is a lad; the 's is read as has
a yen is a longing, an itch

explanation.surface: Someone is told to begin with Japanese money that a boy has put by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yen' looks like Japanese currency; it means a desire.
explanation.definitionFit: To set a machine going you switch it on, which is to start it.

clue.text: We short-circuited race?

parts.note: the newspaper speaks as we, and its short name is also that of a race run on a circuit, the Indianapolis 500

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they disrupted a race by causing an electrical fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We' is The Independent, the paper carrying this puzzle, whose nickname is a shortened form; split 'short-circuited' to read 'We short' and 'circuited race'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Independent is nicknamed this, and the Indianapolis 500 motor race, run on an oval circuit, goes by the same short name.

clue.text: Chopped and changed it in East Germany twice

indicators.note: in says the it letters sit inside the doubled pair
twice means the East and Germany letters appear two times

parts.note: D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: Something was altered and repeated in the former East Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East Germany' looks like the old state; here it is two separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: An edited text has been cut and altered, as an editor trims and revises it.

clue.text: Insured flyer flies, not needing manual?

indicators.note: flies suggests letters scattering through the air, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An insured pilot takes to the air without a handbook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flies' looks like the pilot's action but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy-to-use equipment needs no instruction book, which is what this adjective describes.

clue.text: Bishop cuts canon's cash in Crimea

indicators.note: cuts means the bishop letter slices into the middle of the canon word

parts.note: a canon is a rule or law, with 's read as is
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop reduces a cathedral canon's money while in Crimea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canon' looks like a clergyman beside the bishop; here it means a rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia's currency, also spelt rouble, is used in Crimea since its annexation in 2014.

clue.text: Started to lose heart and pulse

indicators.note: losing heart means the middle letter of the word goes

parts.note: began means started

explanation.surface: Someone began to feel discouraged and their heartbeat changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' looks like a heartbeat but is an edible seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are edible seeds of legumes, and a bean is one such seed.

clue.text: Province's queen bee regularly wearing silk

indicators.note: wearing means the silk is put on around the letters

parts.note: a QC, Queen's Counsel, is called a silk after the silk gown worn

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: A province's queen bee is dressed in silk.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking every second letter of 'queen bee' gives UEBE.
explanation.definitionFit: Quebec is a French-speaking province in eastern Canada.

clue.text: Royalty now and then gets hard biscuits

indicators.note: now and then means only occasional letters, every other one, are kept

parts.note: mud cakes when it dries and hardens

explanation.surface: Royalty sometimes receives tough biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: Every second letter of 'Royalty' gives OAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatcakes are savoury flat biscuits made from oatmeal, popular in Scotland.

clue.text: Warmed up, he put away wine bottles

indicators.note: bottles means the wine word holds the others inside it

parts.note: red is a colour of wine
to put away food is to eat it, so ate

explanation.surface: After warming up, a man stashes wine bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' looks like a noun about wine but is a verb meaning contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Reheated food has been made hot again after cooling.

clue.text: Cook cut unimportant piece of game

parts.note: to do food is to cook it, as in done to a turn

indicators.note: cut means the last letter of the following word is removed

parts.note: minor means unimportant

explanation.surface: A chef chops up an insignificant piece of game meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' suggests venison; it means a board game.
explanation.definitionFit: A domino is one of the small tiles used to play dominoes.
